# Simulating sampling distributions {.unnumbered} This session reproduces what you did with the class reaction-time sheet, then extends it. The simulated population is a class of 500 students rather than 30, which lets us take many more samples than the room allowed. ## Reproduce the draw in code {#sec-code-draw} The code below draws a random sample of 20 students from the population and computes the mean of their reaction times. In the workshop you used 6; we start with 20 here and change it later. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: predict, then run** :::: ::::{.task-container} Read the code below. Before you run it, predict: will the sample mean be exactly equal to the population mean? Write your prediction down. :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sample <- sample(rt_population, size = 20) mean(my_sample) ``` ::: Now repeat the draw many times and collect the means. This builds the same distribution you saw on the board, but with more repetitions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sample_means <- replicate(1000, { s <- sample(rt_population, size = 20) mean(s) }) ggplot(tibble(sample_mean = sample_means), aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#4477AA", colour = "white") + geom_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#EE6677", linewidth = 0.8 ) + labs(x = "Sample mean (ms)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sampling distribution of the mean from 1,000 repeated samples of 20 students.](session-01-computation_files/figure-html/fig-sampling-dist-1.png){#fig-sampling-dist width=672} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: change the sample size** :::: ::::{.task-container} In the code above, change `size = 20` to `size = 50`. **Before you run it, predict:** will the histogram get wider, narrower, or stay the same? Run the code and check. Now change it to `size = 6`, the sample size you used in the workshop, and compare the width with the spread of means on the class board. :::: ::: ## Axis exercise {#sec-axes} The figure below shows two histograms. One shows the distribution of individual reaction times (all 500 students in the population). The other shows the sampling distribution you just built. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Top: distribution of individual reaction times. Bottom: sampling distribution of the mean (n = 20, 1,000 repetitions).](session-01-computation_files/figure-html/fig-thousand-1.png){#fig-thousand fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: read the axes** :::: ::::{.task-container} Look at @fig-thousand and answer the following questions. 1. On the **top** histogram, what does one bar represent?
Each bar is a count of individual students whose reaction time falls in that range. One "observation" on this histogram is one student.
2. On the **bottom** histogram, what does one bar represent?
Each bar is a count of sample means that fell in that range. One "observation" on this histogram is the mean of a sample of 20 students — not a single student.
3. Why is the top histogram wider than the bottom?
Averaging 20 students reduces the variability. Extreme individual values are diluted by the other 19 students in the sample. The distribution of means is always narrower than the distribution of individual values.
:::: ::: ## Generalise beyond the mean {#sec-median} The sampling distribution idea is not special to the mean. Any statistic computed from a random sample is itself random. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: one-word edit** :::: ::::{.task-container} In the sampling distribution code from @sec-code-draw, change `mean(s)` to `median(s)`. Run the code. The histogram you see is the sampling distribution of the **median**. The shape may differ from the mean's, but the principle is the same: a statistic varies from sample to sample. :::: ::: ## Bias contrast {#sec-bias} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: predict before you look** :::: ::::{.task-container} Suppose that entering a score on the class sheet had been optional, and students were more likely to enter it the faster it was (because those are the scores people are pleased with). **Write down your prediction:** will the distribution of sample means shift left, shift right, or stay in the same place? :::: ::: The code below simulates both a blind draw and a speed-biased draw. In the biased version, each student's probability of being selected falls off steeply with their reaction time, so fast students are drawn far more often than slow ones. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} blind_means <- replicate(1000, { s <- sample(rt_population, size = 20) mean(s) }) # Faster students more likely to have entered a score biased_means <- replicate(1000, { s <- sample(rt_population, size = 20, prob = exp(-rt_population / 25)) mean(s) }) bind_rows( tibble(sample_mean = blind_means, draw = "Blind"), tibble(sample_mean = biased_means, draw = "Speed-biased") ) |> ggplot(aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#4477AA", colour = "white") + geom_vline( xintercept = pop_mean, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#EE6677", linewidth = 0.8 ) + facet_wrap(~draw) + labs(x = "Sample mean (ms)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` :::
::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sampling distributions from blind (left) and speed-biased (right) draws.](session-01-computation_files/figure-html/fig-bias-1.png){#fig-bias width=672} ::: :::
:::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: interpret the contrast** :::: ::::{.task-container} Look at @fig-bias. The dashed line is the population mean. 1. Which draw produces a sampling distribution centred on the population mean? 2. Which problem — imprecision or bias — is visible in the speed-biased panel? 3. If you increased the sample size from 20 to 200, would the bias in the right panel disappear?
Bias is a property of the sampling method, not the sample size. Drawing 200 students with a preference for fast ones still underestimates the mean. More data make the estimate more precise (the histogram gets narrower) but do not correct a systematic error in how the sample was collected.
:::: ::: The code that generates the blind draw is: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} blind_means <- replicate(1000, { s <- sample(rt_population, size = 20) mean(s) }) ``` ::: The biased draw adds `prob = exp(-rt_population / 25)`, which weights selection heavily towards faster students: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} biased_means <- replicate(1000, { s <- sample(rt_population, size = 20, prob = exp(-rt_population / 25)) mean(s) }) ``` ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: read the code** :::: ::::{.task-container} Compare the two code blocks above. The only difference is the `prob` argument. State in one sentence what that argument does and why it creates bias.
Use R's inbuilt help functions first trying typing `help(sample)` or `??sample` into the **Console**
The `prob` argument makes each student's **probability of selection decrease steeply with their reaction time**, so faster students are drawn far more often. This shifts the sampling distribution below the true population mean — the same effect as a sheet that only the students with fast scores bothered to fill in.
:::: ::: ## Stretch: the generating process (optional) {#sec-stretch} So far the population has been a fixed sheet of 500 students. But in practice you rarely know every member of the population. Instead you assume the data come from a **process** described by a distribution. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: swap the population for a process** :::: ::::{.task-container} So far you have sampled from a fixed list of 500 students. In real research you almost never have the whole population. Instead, you assume the data come from a **process**: a rule that can generate as many values as you ask for. `rexp(n, rate = 1)` is one such process. Each time it runs, it produces `n` new random values. Most are small and a few are much larger, so the shape is skewed to the right, like reaction times. The values sit around 1 rather than around 250 ms, so expect the numbers on the x-axis to change. **Step 1: look at individual values.** In the code below, replace `rt_population` with `rexp(500, rate = 1)`. This swaps the 500 students for 500 values made by the process. Run it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(tibble(x = rt_population), aes(x = x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#CCBB44", colour = "white") + labs(x = "Individual value", y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: - Are the individual values normally distributed? **Step 2: look at the means.** Go back to the sampling distribution code from @sec-code-draw. Right now each repeat picks 20 students from the list. Replace `sample(rt_population, size = 20)` with `rexp(20, rate = 1)`, so each repeat generates 20 fresh values from the process instead. Run it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sample_means <- replicate(1000, { s <- sample(rt_population, size = 20) # <- replace this line's right-hand side mean(s) }) ggplot(tibble(sample_mean = sample_means), aes(x = sample_mean)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#4477AA", colour = "white") + labs(x = "Sample mean", y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: - Is the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal?
Both histograms come from the same process. The individual values are strongly skewed to the right, but when you average them in groups of 20, the means pile up into a roughly symmetrical, bell-shaped distribution. This is no coincidence, and we will explore this more next time.

What else do you need before you can say how far this is likely to be from the population mean? :::: ::: ## Reading {#sec-reading} - ["Sampling Distribution: Definition, Formula & Examples"](statisticsbyjim.com/hypothesis-testing/sampling-distribution/). Covers what a sampling distribution is, uses a repeated-sampling simulation with apples, shows histograms of sample means, and demonstrates how the distribution changes with sample size. - ["Sample Statistics Are Always Wrong (to Some Extent)!"](statisticsbyjim.com/basics/sample-statistics-wrong/).
